newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.KOREAN FIRMS TRANSSHIPPING GOLD TO USE DLR FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: S.KOREAN FIRMS TRANSSHIPPING GOLD TO USE DLR FUNDS.

text.p: Fourteen South Korean companies were found to have transshipped 329.19 tonnes of gold bullion in calendar 1996 to secure dollar funds, the independent Board of Audit and Inspection said on Monday.
It compared to South Korea's total gold imports of 424.4 tonnes in 1996, including gold in unwrought, semi-manufactured or powder form and of 24K gold coins.
The board said in a report the companies imported gold on 90-day deferred payment terms and then re-exported it within the next one to six days without any reprocessing procedure.
Such irregular, but not illegal, transactions enabled them to employ the dollar funds for up to 90 days until they had to pay for imports, the report said.
Such re-exports worth $4.1 billion were included in the annual export volume of the companies, thereby distorting their export performance, the report said.
The board did not name the companies.
Last year, South Korean gold imports were 95.2 percent more than the previous year's 217.4 tonnes, according to the central Bank of Korea's statistics.
New rules limiting deferred payments on imports to 30 days were put into effect in July 1996, but recently South Korea's gold transshipment trade has begun to rise.
A central Bank of Korea official said South Korea's gold imports had surged 25.6 percent to 304 tonnes in the first half of 1997.
Traders said some local companies had found a loophole in the new rules and were now requiring advance payments on gold exports of as much as 120 days from foreign buyers.
That, added to the current 30 days of deferred payments on imports, would give local bullion houses control of funds for a maximum of 150 days.
